📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when it comes to the Thanksgiving feast, Americans' favorite sides include mashed potatoes, green bean casserole, and of course, stuffing. Whether it comes from a box or is lovingly homemade, stuffing is a filling, savory, and surprisingly historical part of many Turkey Day spreads. And there are seemingly as many variations of stuffing as there are households in the U.S., but butter is a unifying and necessary ingredient that no version of this Thanksgiving side can go without. However, if you really want to up the richness and flavor of your next casserole dish of stuffing, forget plain old regular butter and instead try brown butter.

Industry observers note that brown butter is most notably used in sweet baked goods, but the golden, nutty version can truly enhance pretty much anything where regular butter is used, including savory dishes like stuffing. What it adds to your T-giving side is a sumptuous, caramelly flavor that creates a world of depth and complexity, as the sweetness of the brown butter beautifully complements all the savory ingredients in the stuffing, like the softened bread cubes, sausage (if you use any), and the fresh herbs.

Don't skimp on it, either. If you're going to use brown butter in stuffing, you'll need to start with quite a bit of butter, perhaps as much as two to three full sticks, because the flavors in your typical stuffing can be bold, and you want to be able to taste the butterscotch-y nuttiness, which pairs so well with sage and onion, or the mushroom in a classic sausage and mushroom stuffing. Even if you make a pumpkin and herb stuffing, full of warming spices and chili, brown butter will enhance the subtle sweetness of the pumpkin and the juiciness of the raisins.

Industry observers note that if you're inspired to try using brown butter in your stuffing this year for Thanksgiving, but you've never made it before and you're a little intimidated by it, we've a few tips to get you started. First thing, the color of the pan you use matters because you'll want to keep a close eye on how dark the butter is getting — hard to do in cast iron. The choice is yours whether you use salted or unsalted butter, but you'll want to adjust the seasonings in your stuffing accordingly. It's vital that you don't use too high a heat; a good medium to medium-low will do the trick. And finally, don't walk away while your butter is browning because the process is quick, and you can go from delectably golden brown with a nutty aroma to burnt and bitter in a hurry.

According to recent reports, there are a number of ways to incorporate brown butter into your stuffing, and whichever you choose, you'll want to remove the pan off the heat as soon as the butter is ready. You might add the veggies, aromatics, and herbs directly into the brown butter pan and let those saturate and saute in the nutty goodness, then add them to the bread element. Or you can remove the brown butter from the pan and keep it aside in a bowl, saute the vegetables, add everything into the waiting bowl of butter, and toss to combine.

Give Burgers A Protein Boost By Adding One Canned Ingredient To Ground Beef

💡 Key Takeaways
  • When you need protein to help support your body after a workout or to keep you satiated throughout the day, you can reach for a number of foods, but we'd venture that there isn't a tastier option than a hamburger or cheeseburger.
  • Depending on the type of bean you use, a half-cup typically contains between 7 and 9 grams of protein that you can add to your meat mixture, and ultimately, black beans would be our first choice.
  • Recent findings suggest that canned beans are often packed in a gooey liquid that consists of the starches and other substances that seep out of the beans, mixed with water and sometimes a bit of salt.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When you need protein to help support your body after a workout or to keep you satiated throughout the day, you can reach for a number of foods, but we'd venture that there isn't a tastier option than a hamburger or cheeseburger. There are plenty of fast food options that are positively awash in the macronutrient, but cooking at home gives you far more control. Now, ground beef is obviously chock-full of protein, with anywhere from 16 to 24 grams per 4-ounce serving, but if you have a serious goal you need to meet before EOD, there is a canned ingredient that is probably lurking in your pantry (and if it isn't, it should be) that can help push you over the edge. It's beans!

Depending on the type of bean you use, a half-cup typically contains between 7 and 9 grams of protein that you can add to your meat mixture, and ultimately, black beans would be our first choice. Not only are they closest in color to a perfectly grilled burger, but they're surprisingly meaty. When they're mashed and mixed in with the ground beef, they blend right in, and their mild flavor means they take on whatever seasonings you include without drawing attention to themselves (oh, and there's the added bonus that, in addition to the extra protein, they're also a high-fiber food). By the way, if you don't have black beans on hand, you can absolutely use pinto, cannellini, or even red kidney beans.

Recent findings suggest that canned beans are often packed in a gooey liquid that consists of the starches and other substances that seep out of the beans, mixed with water and sometimes a bit of salt. As such, they are too wet straight out of the can to use in your burger mixture, so you should drain them and then dry them as much as you can (otherwise, your patties could be a soggy mess). You can even help the process by wicking as much moisture out of them as possible, making for a much more desirable texture, by placing them in a single layer on a baking sheet and popping them in the oven for a few minutes.

In a recent development, mashing the beans by hand before adding them to the ground beef will always be preferable to the evisceration they'd receive in a food processor. Taking a potato masher (or you could use your meat chopper from the Dollar Tree) to the beans produces a variety of different shapes, which is useful not just for aesthetic purposes (the irregularities in the beans mimic the natural lumps that form when burger patties cook), but also for a more satisfyingly hearty bite.

Now, beans and ground beef alone do not a burger patty make; you may want to include some binders to help hold everything together. This might be as simple as an egg or two and breadcrumbs — which type of breadcrumbs is totally up to you, because typical fine-textured crumbs will work, as will panko — plus a condiment of your choice, like ketchup, mustard, or even tangy barbecue sauce.

For The Best Scrambled Eggs With Extra Fiber, Make Them Turkish Style

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, getting your morning fiber doesn't have to be all about eating more fruits or specialty yogurts.
  • In a recent development, A proper menemen is customizable, but always requires three things: eggs, tomatoes, and peppers.
  • This is without even mentioning the fiber in the peppers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, getting your morning fiber doesn't have to be all about eating more fruits or specialty yogurts. Instead, you can deliciously upgrade your scrambled eggs with classic Turkish vegetables in menemen, a sort of low-effort dish that comes loaded with nutrients.

In a recent development, A proper menemen is customizable, but always requires three things: eggs, tomatoes, and peppers. It lets you get so much fiber because it starts with sauteing the vegetables until they soften and reduce in size, so you can load up quite a bit in a single meal. While the exact nutritional profile varies between different types of tomatoes, there's an average of about 2.16 grams of fiber per cup. The sauteing step means you can easily add two cups and cook them down to a thick, jammy consistency, providing a delicious brightness to the eggs just over 4 grams of fiber all in one go.

This is without even mentioning the fiber in the peppers. Banana peppers are relatively high in fiber, clocking in at around 4 grams per cup. Bell peppers are also quite tasty, with some varieties providing about 3 grams per cup. Since the recommended daily fiber intake for most adults hovers between 25 and 38 grams, you could potentially get a substantial portion of your daily needs all in one go. And unlike shakshuka and eggs in purgatory, two similar dishes that traditionally rely on poaching or braising, menemen lets you control the texture quite easily, whether you like your eggs creamy, fluffy, or dense.

In a recent development, between the rich flavors of menemen and the plethora of foods it can pair with, you've got ample room to deliciously add even more fiber to your breakfast. Taking inspiration from a traditional Turkish breakfast is a great place to start, but don't be afraid to treat your menemen as a starting point rather than a set-in-stone recipe.

In a recent development, like many countries, Turkey is a major believer in some early morning carbs, and bread products are a great way to add a bit more fiber to your diet. While a slice of white bread may be versatile and provide some sweetness to round out the tomatoes' acidity, one slice also only has about 0.6 grams of fiber. Instead, look to rye, a bread that may not be for everyone but can have three times the fiber of white bread. A slice of pumpernickel can even add 2.7 more grams of fiber to your morning, and the rich, earthy aromas and dense texture are a great contrast to creamy eggs and veggies.

Few fruits are quite so high in fiber as avocado, with a single medium-sized fruit containing around 10 grams of fiber. As a topping for menemen, its rich creaminess works perfectly with the sharper vegetable flavors, while the eggs provide plenty of protein. Half an avocado smeared over pumpernickel and topped with menemen could provide around 16 grams of fiber from all the different sources, roughly half of what many people need per day.

#22876. 25 types of meditation and how to choose the right one

25 types of meditation and how to choose the right one

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3246 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • Recent findings suggest that the benefits of meditation can reach across your well-being, from reducing stress and anxiety to improving focus and supporting mental and emotional health.
  • We’ve grouped the many types of meditation into six families, so you can see how they relate before you pick one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA.

Recent findings suggest that the benefits of meditation can reach across your well-being, from reducing stress and anxiety to improving focus and supporting mental and emotional health. But there’s a catch: meditation is a wide family of practices, and the type that works beautifully for your friend might leave you fidgety and frustrated.

We’ve grouped the many types of meditation into six families, so you can see how they relate before you pick one. Think of it as a menu. Try whichever one draws you in, and let your practice change as you do.

Meditation is a way to train our attention and awareness so we can be more present in the moment. Most types ask you to rest your focus somewhere, like the breath, a word, a sensation, or a movement, and to notice without judgment when your mind drifts, then return. That returning, over and over, is the practice.

In a recent development, what changes from one type to the next is where you place your attention and what you hope to cultivate. Some practices sharpen focus, while others cultivate compassion or help the body relax. Many share a thread of mindfulness, noticing where your attention drifts and gently coming back.

With a history rooted in the spiritual traditions of the East, including Buddhism, Hinduism, and Taoism, meditation has long been recognized as a means to gain enlightenment, self-realization, and balance.

By exploring the different forms of meditation practice, you can discover what works best for you to enhance your overall well-being.

Recent findings suggest that these practices share a common aim. You anchor your attention in the present moment and meet whatever arises without judgment. They're a good place to start if you're newly introduced to meditation.

In a recent development, particularly accessible to beginners, mindfulness meditation invites you to immerse yourself in the present moment. It teaches you to observe your thoughts, feelings, and physical sensations without judgment. By focusing on the breath or the sensations in the body, rather than worries about the past or future, you learn to anchor yourself in the now. This can lead to reduced stress and improved well-being.

Read more: How to practice mindfulness meditation: 8 tips to get started.

Recent findings suggest that A body scan moves your attention slowly through the body, one area at a time, noticing sensation without trying to change it. It's a core mindfulness technique and a gentle way into the practice, since you always have your body to come back to. Many people use it to unwind before sleep.

Read more: Body scan meditation: a step-by-step guide to practice.

Here the breath is your anchor. You rest your attention on each inhale and exhale, without trying to control the rhythm, and return to it whenever your mind wanders. Because your breath is always with you, this is one of the most portable practices you can carry into a stressful moment.

Read more: How to practice breath meditation to relieve stress.

It has been revealed that mindful eating brings full attention to a meal through the senses: the color, smell, texture, and taste of your food, and the signals of hunger and fullness. It can support digestion and help you notice emotional eating patterns with more kindness.

Read more: How mindful eating can boost your mental and physical health.

Focus is the whole point here. You rest your attention on one thing, a flame, a sound, or a word, and return to it each time the mind strays. Over time this can sharpen your attention and prepare you for deeper states.

Sources indicate that concentration meditation is a practice of focused attention, where the mind is directed toward a single point of reference, such as a candle flame, a sound, or the breath. This can help develop focus and attentiveness in everyday life and prepare the mind for deeper states of meditation. This practice can be especially helpful for students, professionals, or anyone looking to improve their cognitive abilities and productivity.

Read more: Concentration meditation: what is it and how to practice?

Recent findings suggest that mantra meditation involves the silent repetition of a word or phrase, known as a mantra, to focus the mind and bring deeper states of meditation. This practice can be found in many spiritual traditions worldwide and serves as a powerful tool for calming the mind, reducing stress, and enhancing spiritual growth and a sense of peace and clarity. If you find yourself easily distracted or struggling with a busy mind, mantra meditation can help you maintain focus.

Read more: Mantra meditation: what it is, benefits, and how to practice.

Om meditation is a form of mantra practice built around chanting or silently repeating the sound "Om." The vibration of the sound gives the mind something to settle on, and many practitioners find the repetition grounding.

Industry observers note that read more: What is Om meditation? Plus, a step-by-step guide to practice.

Also called trataka, candle meditation uses the soft glow of a flame as your focal point. You rest your gaze on the candle, placed at eye level a short distance away, and let it hold your attention. It's a visual anchor for anyone who finds eyes-closed practice restless.

Read more: Candle meditation: a step-by-step guide to practice at home.

Industry observers note that visualization meditation guides you to picture a scene, place, or outcome in vivid detail, such as somewhere you feel calm and safe. By giving the mind a rich image to rest on, it can lower stress and support a sense of ease. Unlike open mindfulness, it actively directs the imagination.

Read more: Visualization meditation: 8 exercises to add to your practice.

Warmth is the thread running through this family, directed toward yourself, the people you love, and even those you struggle with. These practices can enhance empathy and strengthen your relationships.

Compassion meditation aims to cultivate feelings of love, kindness, and compassion toward yourself and others. It involves silently directing sentiments of goodwill toward loved ones, acquaintances, and even people we might have a difficult relationship with. It encourages us to see beyond our differences, nurturing a sense of connectedness. A traditional example is Tonglen, a Tibetan practice that pairs the breath with compassion for suffering.

Read more: Compassion meditation: what it is, benefits, & how to practice.

It has been revealed that 11. Loving-kindness meditation (metta).

Loving-kindness, or Metta meditation, is a practice of cultivating an attitude of unconditional love and kindness towards all beings. It starts with developing a loving acceptance of yourself and gradually extends outward to include friends, family, strangers, and even those with whom we may have conflicts. This practice can help break down barriers of anger and division, promoting peace and connection. Though loving-kindness meditation and compassion meditation are closely related and often practiced together, loving-kindness meditation involves sending wishes of happiness, well-being, and peace to yourself and others, whereas compassion meditation specifically focuses on suffering, understanding it, feeling it, and wishing for it to be alleviated.

Read more: Loving-kindness meditation: what it is, how to practice and why.

Gratitude meditation guides your attention toward what you appreciate, often by calling to mind a few people or moments you're thankful for. Practiced in the morning or evening, it can lower anxiety and support better sleep, and it pairs naturally with compassion practice.

Read more: How gratitude meditation can help reduce anxiety.

Recent findings suggest that sitting still doesn't suit everyone. If stillness makes you restless, these practices let you meditate while the body is in motion, with your attention on each movement.

Sources indicate that moving meditation brings together deliberate movement and a focused mind. You move with purpose, noticing each step, stretch, or breath as you go. Yoga, tai chi, mindful stretching, and mindful dancing all fall under this heading, and it can be done almost anywhere.

Read more: The benefits of moving meditation and how to start practicing.

Recent findings suggest that walking meditation means walking slowly and deliberately, with your attention fully on the act of walking: each step, the movement of your legs, the ground beneath your feet, and your breath. It turns an everyday activity into a practice you can take outdoors.

Read more: Walking meditation: how to practice and its benefits.

Mindful movement is the broad practice of bringing present-moment awareness to how your body moves, whether through stretching, yoga, or simple everyday motion. It's mindfulness carried into the body rather than held in stillness.

Recent findings suggest that read more: What is mindful movement? Plus 9 ways to get started.

Qigong is a traditional Chinese practice that combines movement, breathwork, and meditation to support balance and focus. In its active form you meditate while flowing through slow, deliberate movements, which makes it a bridge between exercise and stillness.

Recent findings suggest that read more: What is qigong? Benefits, types, and how to practice.

Yoga nidra, sometimes called yogic sleep, is a guided rest practice done lying down. A teacher or recording leads you through stages of body scan, breath, and visualization into a state between waking and sleep. No yoga experience is needed, and it's often used for deep rest at bedtime.

Read more: What is yoga nidra? Plus, why it may be your latest BFF at bedtime.

A few practices are rooted in a specific lineage and tend to go deeper, often taught within a tradition or by a teacher. Several come from Buddhism, while others, like Transcendental Meditation and kundalini, come from Hindu and Vedic traditions.

Buddhist meditation is the broad tradition behind many of the best-known techniques, including Zen and Vipassana below, along with loving-kindness. If you want a feel for the tradition as a whole before exploring the specific practices, start here.

Read more: Buddhist meditation: types, techniques & how to practice.

Industry observers note that zen meditation, or Zazen, is a disciplined form of meditation central to Zen Buddhism. You sit in a specific posture, focusing on the breath while observing thoughts and sensations as they arise and pass without attachment. Zazen emphasizes the importance of moment-to-moment awareness for a profound sense of peace and insight.

Read more: Zen meditation: how (and why) to start a Zen practice.

Vipassana, which means "to see things as they really are," is one of India's most ancient techniques of meditation. It focuses on the deep interconnection between mind and body. Through disciplined attention to physical sensations, you can develop insight into the nature of impermanence, suffering, and egolessness, to move toward enlightenment and liberation. Vipassana meditation is challenging, yet rewarding, offering profound insights into our own minds.

Read more: Vipassana meditation: what it is, benefits & how to practice.

Sources indicate that 21. Transcendental Meditation (TM).

According to recent reports, transcendental Meditation comes from the Hindu and Vedic tradition and was brought to the West in the mid-20th century. It's a silent, mantra-based practice, typically done for about 20 minutes twice a day, and it's taught one-on-one by a certified teacher who gives you your mantra. It's described as effortless, letting the mantra gently carry the mind toward deep rest.

Read more: Transcendental Meditation versus mindfulness meditation.

Kundalini meditation is a spiritual practice that aims to awaken what the tradition describes as an inner energy at the base of the spine, using breathwork, posture, and chanting. Practitioners describe effects in spiritual and energetic terms, which are rooted in belief rather than established science. Because the breathwork can be intense, check with your doctor first if you have respiratory, heart, or blood pressure concerns.

Sources indicate that read more: What is Kundalini meditation? Plus, how to try it yourself.

In a recent development, chakra meditation focuses attention on the body's energy centers, or chakras, often by visualizing each as a spinning wheel, chanting a sound for each one, or breathing into each area. As with kundalini, the idea of chakras comes from spiritual tradition and is described as belief rather than scientific fact.

Read more: Chakra meditation: what it is, benefits & how to practice.

Recent findings suggest that this family works from the body inward. The practices help your nervous system slow down and your muscles release tension, which makes them a good entry point when stress reveals up physically.

In a recent development, relaxation meditation is an umbrella term for any practice that helps the body release tension and the mind wind down. It often draws on breathing, body awareness, or guided sessions, and it's a gentle place to begin if deeper practices feel like a lot right now.

A sound bath, where you lie back and listen to instruments, is one example.

Read more: 5 relaxation meditations that actually work.

In a recent development, 25. Progressive muscle relaxation.

Progressive muscle relaxation guides you to tense and then release each muscle group in turn, usually working from the feet up to the face. By targeting the physical side of stress, it can ease tension that anxiety stores in the body, and it pairs well with a body scan to finish.

Read more: What is progressive muscle relaxation (and how to practice it).

According to recent reports, the six families above group the 25 types by where your attention goes. This table puts them side by side, so you can compare meditation types and see where to start.

There’s no one-size-fits-all approach to meditation, and your needs may change over time. The best meditation technique is the one that feels right for you now and fits into your life. These five steps can help you find it.

Sources indicate that reflect on your goals: Think about what you're hoping to achieve. Whether it's reducing stress, finding inner peace, or developing compassion, your goals can guide your choice of practice.

Experiment with different practices: Try out different meditation methods and resources, including the Calm app, online courses, and local meditation groups, for guided sessions in different styles.

Recent findings suggest that listen to your body and mind: Pay attention to how you feel during and after meditation. The right practice should leave you feeling calm and refreshed. If you feel frustrated or strained, try a different type.

Recent findings suggest that be patient and open-minded: Finding the meditation practice that works for you can take time. Approach each type with curiosity, allowing your experiences to guide your journey.

Seek guidance: If you're unsure where to start, seek advice from experienced practitioners or meditation teachers for support tailored to your personal journey.

Starting a meditation practice can bring greater mindfulness and improved emotional well-being. However, establishing a consistent practice can feel daunting. By bringing these tips into your approach, you can build a meditation practice that fits your life and becomes a source of strength and peace.

Industry observers note that A consistent routine is vital in establishing any new habit, including meditation. Identify a time of day when you can dedicate a few uninterrupted minutes to your practice. For many, morning meditation sets a positive tone for the day ahead. However, if evenings or another time fits your schedule better, make that your meditation moment. Find a quiet, comfortable spot where you can sit or lie down without distractions.

💙 Morning person? Try this Morning Meditation to set your tone for the rest of the day. Nighttime person? This Deep Rest meditation is for you.

Begin with just a few minutes each day. Even a short period of meditation can have significant benefits, and starting small makes the practice feel more manageable. As you become more comfortable with the process, you can gradually extend your meditation time.

💙 Begin your meditation journey with Jeff Warren in this Meditation for Beginners series.

Meditation is a personal experience, and there’s no single "right" way to do it. Many people form expectations based on others' descriptions, but each person's meditation journey is unique. You don’t need to empty your mind or feel bliss in every session. Notice your thoughts and feelings without judgment, and meet whatever comes up with kindness and curiosity.

💙 Explore how having Expectations can affect us and our lives with Tamara Levitt on the Daily Calm.

Recent findings suggest that physical discomfort can be a distraction during meditation. To help settle your body and prepare for stillness, consider some gentle stretching or mindful movement, such as yoga or tai chi, before you begin. This can help release tension in the body and allow you to sit more comfortably.

💙 Follow along with The Daily Move’s Releasing Stress session to help you unwind before settling down.

Sources indicate that guided meditations, available through apps, websites, or local classes, can provide verbal instructions and cues to lead you through the meditation process. They can introduce you to different types of meditation, help keep your focus, and offer insights into how to handle common challenges like wandering thoughts or restlessness.

💙 Try this guided meditation to help you with Reframing Difficult Thoughts whenever your thoughts start to overwhelm you.

Sources indicate that it’s normal to encounter challenges as you begin your meditation practice. You might miss a day or find your mind wandering constantly. When this happens, treat yourself with kindness and compassion. Each time you notice your mind has drifted and come back to the present moment, you’re practicing.

💙 Practice this Loving Kindness meditation to guide you in cultivating feelings of kindness toward yourself and others.

Join a meditation group or find a community of practitioners that can provide support and a sense of connection. Sharing experiences with others on a similar path can be incredibly encouraging.

There’s no single agreed list, but these three approaches are often used to sort the many types of meditation:.

Recent findings suggest that concentration meditation: You rest your attention on a single point of reference, such as the breath, a mantra, a sound, or a candle flame. When your mind wanders, you return to it.

Mindfulness meditation: You widen your awareness to include thoughts, sensations, and your surroundings as they arise. It is often taught as part of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR).

Loving-kindness meditation (Metta): You build goodwill and warmth toward others, starting with yourself.

Industry observers note that the idea of levels in meditation can vary depending on the tradition or practice. A way to think of meditation depth might include the different types and states.

Physical relaxation: The initial stage where the body relaxes deeply.

Concentration: The mind begins to focus, reducing distractions.

Mindful awareness: A state of heightened awareness of the present moment.

Deepening peace: Inner silence becomes more profound.

Insight: Understanding about yourself and reality may arise.

Blissful states: Experiences of joy or profound contentment.

Transcendence: A sense of unity or oneness with all, often considered the deepest level of meditation.

The power of a meditation practice can vary from person to person, depending on individual needs, preferences, and goals. Some may find mindfulness meditation helpful for managing stress and enhancing self-awareness, while others prefer the structured approach of Transcendental Meditation or the heart-opening practices of loving-kindness meditation.

Ultimately, the most ‘powerful’ type is the one you’ll keep practicing. Try a few to see which fits.
